Question
========
Draw a proper graph that approximates the latency of: a register, L1 and L2 cache, DRAM, an HDD, a transfer over WiFi, and the picture of (1) a cute cat that is very trendy on Instagram and (2) a picture of a random cat that nobody has seen yet, just published by someone in the USA.

The X axis is the approximate distance from the CPU control unit to the item. The Y axis is free but should be chosen wisely.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.6, fig.height=5.0}
par(mar=c(0,0,0,0)); plot.new(); plot.window(c(0,100),c(0,100))
rect(1,1,99,99)
arrows(12,10,94,10,length=.1); arrows(12,10,12,92,length=.1)
text(53,5,"Distance from the control unit",cex=.8); text(6,50,"Latency",srt=90,cex=.8)
```

Solution
========
The Y axis must be latency on a logarithmic scale, since the values span more than ten orders of magnitude, and the X axis, distance, is best logarithmic too. The points then line up on a rising curve.

- Register: inside the core, under a nanometre scale distance, about 0.3 ns.
- L1: a few mm, about 1 ns. L2: about a cm, about 4 ns.
- DRAM: a few cm, about 80 ns.
- HDD: tens of cm inside the case, about 10 ms, dominated by the seek and not by the distance.
- WiFi: a few metres, about 1 to 10 ms.
- The trendy cat: served by a CDN cache nearby, tens of km, about 10 to 30 ms.
- The fresh cat from the USA: no CDN copy yet, so it must be fetched across the Atlantic, about 6000 km, about 100 to 150 ms.

The point of the last two items is that they are at the same logical place but not at the same physical one: caching is what makes distance disappear, and a brand new object has not been cached anywhere yet.
